title: IRS Tax Brackets 2025: What Every American Needs to Know
excerpt: The IRS released updated tax brackets for 2025 with inflation adjustments. Here is a clear breakdown of every rate and what it means for your paycheck.
content:
The IRS announced the 2025 tax brackets in Revenue Procedure 2024-40, adjusting all thresholds for inflation. Understanding which bracket you fall into helps you plan withholding, estimated payments, and year-end moves.

2025 Tax Rates for Single Filers

  • 10% on income up to $11,925
  • 12% on $11,926 – $48,475
  • 22% on $48,476 – $103,350
  • 24% on $103,351 – $197,300
  • 32% on $197,301 – $250,525
  • 35% on $250,526 – $626,350
  • 37% on income above $626,350

2025 Rates for Married Filing Jointly

  • 10% on income up to $23,850
  • 12% on $23,851 – $96,950
  • 22% on $96,951 – $206,700
  • 24% on $206,701 – $394,600
  • 32% on $394,601 – $501,050
  • 35% on $501,051 – $751,600
  • 37% on income above $751,600

Important: The US Uses a Marginal System

You do not pay your top rate on all income. Each portion of your income is taxed at its corresponding bracket rate. If you are a single filer earning $60,000, only the income above $48,475 is taxed at 22% — the rest is taxed at lower rates.

Source: IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40

title: Standard Deduction 2025: How Much Can You Deduct?
excerpt: The standard deduction increased again for 2025. Most Americans take it instead of itemizing — find out exactly how much you can deduct this year.
content:
The IRS increased the standard deduction for 2025 as part of its annual inflation adjustment under Revenue Procedure 2024-40. For most taxpayers, the standard deduction is larger than their itemized deductions, making it the smarter choice.

2025 Standard Deduction Amounts

  • Single / Married Filing Separately: $15,000
  • Married Filing Jointly: $30,000
  • Head of Household: $22,500

Additional Deduction if 65 or Older / Blind

Taxpayers who are 65 or older, or legally blind, receive an additional deduction:

  • Single: +$2,000
  • Married (per qualifying spouse): +$1,600

Should You Itemize Instead?

Itemizing makes sense only if your deductible expenses — mortgage interest, state and local taxes (capped at $10,000), charitable donations, and medical expenses above 7.5% of AGI — exceed the standard deduction. For most Americans, the standard deduction wins.

Source: IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40

title: Where Is My Tax Refund? How to Track Your IRS Refund Status
excerpt: The IRS Where's My Refund tool gives you a real-time status update. Here is exactly how to use it, what the status messages mean, and when to take action.
content:
The IRS processes most e-filed refunds within 21 days. The fastest way to check your status is the Where's My Refund? tool at IRS.gov or the IRS2Go mobile app.

How to Check Your Refund Status

  1. Go to IRS.gov/refunds
  2. Enter your Social Security number, filing status, and exact refund amount
  3. View your current status

When Can You Check?

  • E-filed return: 24 hours after the IRS acknowledges receipt
  • Paper return: 4 weeks after mailing
  • Amended return (1040-X): 3 weeks after filing

What the Status Messages Mean

  • Return Received: IRS has your return and is processing it
  • Refund Approved: Refund has been approved and will be sent
  • Refund Sent: Direct deposit initiated or check mailed

Why Is My Refund Delayed?

Refunds can be delayed if your return requires additional review, contains errors, is affected by identity theft screening, or claims the EITC or Additional Child Tax Credit (by law, these cannot be issued before mid-February).

Source: IRS.gov/refunds — Where's My Refund?

title: How to File Your Taxes for Free in 2025: IRS Free File Explained
excerpt: Millions of Americans overpay for tax software when they can file completely free through the IRS. Here is who qualifies and exactly how to do it.
content:
The IRS Free File program allows eligible taxpayers to prepare and file their federal tax return at no cost, using brand-name software. In 2024, anyone with an adjusted gross income (AGI) of $84,000 or less qualifies.

How IRS Free File Works

  1. Go to IRS.gov/freefile
  2. Use the Look Up tool to find a software partner that matches your situation
  3. Click the link to go directly to the software — do not search for it separately
  4. Create an account and complete your return
  5. E-file for free — federal filing is always free, some partners offer free state filing too

Free File Fillable Forms (No Income Limit)

If your income exceeds $84,000, you can still use Free File Fillable Forms — electronic versions of IRS paper forms with basic math calculations. These require you to know which forms to use.

Free File vs Free Edition (Commercial Software)

Be careful: commercial software companies often advertise a Free Edition that has income or situation restrictions. IRS Free File is the only program guaranteed free for all eligible filers.

Source: IRS Free File — irs.gov/filing/free-file-do-your-federal-taxes-for-free

title: W-2 vs 1099: What's the Difference and How It Affects Your Taxes
excerpt: Receiving a 1099 instead of a W-2 means the IRS treats you differently. Self-employment tax, quarterly payments, and deductions all change. Here is what you need to know.
content:
Whether you receive a W-2 or a 1099-NEC determines how your income is taxed, how much you owe, and what deductions you can take.

W-2: Employee

Your employer withholds federal and state income tax, Social Security (6.2%), and Medicare (1.45%) from every paycheck. At year-end you receive a W-2 reporting all wages and withholding. You file Schedule W-2 with your 1040.

1099-NEC: Independent Contractor

You receive payment in full — no withholding. You are responsible for paying self-employment tax of 15.3% (covering both the employee and employer share of Social Security and Medicare), plus income tax on net profit. You file Schedule C with your 1040.

Key Differences at a Glance

  • Withholding: W-2 yes, 1099 no
  • SE Tax: W-2 no (split with employer), 1099 yes (full 15.3%)
  • Business deductions: W-2 limited, 1099 full Schedule C deductions
  • Quarterly payments: W-2 usually not needed, 1099 almost always required

Can You Receive Both?

Yes. Many Americans have a W-2 job and freelance income. In that case, you file both Schedule C for the 1099 income and include your W-2 wages on your 1040.

Source: IRS Publication 15-A; IRS.gov/self-employed

title: Crypto Tax Rules: How the IRS Taxes Bitcoin and Digital Assets in 2024
excerpt: The IRS treats cryptocurrency as property, not currency. Every sale, trade, and even some purchases can be a taxable event. Here is how it works.
content:
The IRS classifies cryptocurrency and other digital assets as property under Notice 2014-21. This means general tax principles that apply to property transactions — including capital gains rules — apply to every crypto transaction.

What Counts as a Taxable Event?

  • Selling crypto for US dollars or another fiat currency
  • Trading one cryptocurrency for another (e.g., Bitcoin to Ethereum)
  • Using crypto to buy goods or services
  • Receiving crypto as payment for work (ordinary income)
  • Receiving staking rewards or mining rewards (ordinary income at fair market value)

What Is NOT Taxable?

  • Buying crypto with US dollars and holding it
  • Transferring crypto between your own wallets
  • Receiving crypto as a gift (until you sell)

Short-Term vs Long-Term Capital Gains

If you held the crypto for one year or less before selling, gains are taxed as ordinary income. If held longer than one year, long-term capital gains rates apply (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

How to Report

Report all crypto transactions on Form 8949 and summarize on Schedule D. The IRS added a digital assets question directly on Form 1040 — answer it honestly.

Sources: IRS Notice 2014-21; IRS Revenue Ruling 2023-14; IRS.gov/virtualcurrency

title: IRS Audit Triggers: 10 Red Flags That Increase Your Audit Risk
excerpt: The IRS selects returns for audit based on statistical formulas and specific triggers. Knowing what draws attention can help you file cleaner, more defensible returns.
content:
The IRS audited about 0.38% of individual returns in 2022 (IRS Data Book). But certain items dramatically increase that probability. Here are the top triggers.

Top 10 IRS Audit Triggers

  1. High income: Returns with over $1M in income are audited at far higher rates
  2. Large Schedule C losses: Consistent losses from a business signal a hobby loss issue
  3. Excessive home office deduction: Large deductions relative to income draw scrutiny
  4. Round numbers: Estimates like $5,000 or $10,000 look suspicious — real expenses have cents
  5. Large charitable deductions: Non-cash contributions exceeding $500 require Form 8283
  6. High vehicle use percentage: Claiming 100% business use of a vehicle is a red flag
  7. Unreported income: The IRS receives copies of all 1099s and W-2s — mismatches trigger notices
  8. Foreign bank accounts: Failure to file FBAR or Form 8938 is heavily scrutinized
  9. Cash-intensive businesses: Restaurants, hair salons, and similar businesses face higher audit rates
  10. Math errors and missing forms: Simple errors can trigger correspondence audits automatically

What to Do If Audited

Respond promptly, gather documentation for every deduction, and consider working with an Enrolled Agent or tax professional. Most correspondence audits can be resolved without an in-person meeting.

Sources: IRS Data Book 2023; IRS.gov/audit

title: Self-Employed Tax Deductions: The Complete Guide for 2024
excerpt: Self-employed Americans can deduct far more than most realize. From the SE tax deduction to the 20% QBI deduction, here is every write-off you should know.
content:
As a self-employed individual, you file Schedule C to report business income and expenses. The IRS allows deductions for all ordinary and necessary business expenses. Here are the most valuable ones.

1. Self-Employment Tax Deduction

You can deduct 50% of your self-employment tax from your gross income. This is an above-the-line deduction — you get it even without itemizing.

2. Self-Employed Health Insurance

You can deduct 100% of health insurance premiums for yourself, your spouse, and dependents — as long as you are not eligible for employer coverage through a spouse.

3. Home Office Deduction

If you use a dedicated space exclusively for business, deduct either $5/sq ft (simplified, max 300 sq ft) or actual expenses proportional to office size.

4. Vehicle Expenses

Deduct business miles at the 2024 standard rate of 67 cents per mile, or use the actual expense method (gas, insurance, depreciation).

5. Retirement Contributions

Contribute to a SEP-IRA (up to 25% of net self-employment income, max $69,000 in 2024) or Solo 401(k). These reduce taxable income dollar for dollar.

6. Qualified Business Income (QBI) Deduction

Many self-employed filers can deduct up to 20% of qualified business income under Section 199A. Income limits apply for certain service businesses.

7. Education and Professional Development

Courses, certifications, books, and subscriptions that maintain or improve your business skills are deductible.

Sources: IRS Publication 334; Schedule C Instructions; IRS.gov/self-employed

title: Capital Gains Tax 2024: Rates, Rules, and How to Reduce What You Owe
excerpt: Selling stocks, real estate, or other assets triggers capital gains tax. The rate depends on how long you held the asset and your income. Here is exactly how it works.
content:
A capital gain occurs when you sell an asset for more than you paid. The IRS taxes gains differently based on your holding period.

Short-Term Capital Gains (Held 1 Year or Less)

Taxed as ordinary income at your regular tax bracket rate — as high as 37%.

Long-Term Capital Gains (Held More Than 1 Year)

Preferential rates apply for 2024:

  • 0% — Single income up to $47,025 / MFJ up to $94,050
  • 15% — Single up to $518,900 / MFJ up to $583,750
  • 20% — Above those thresholds

Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT)

High earners (single over $200,000 / MFJ over $250,000) also pay an additional 3.8% NIIT on investment income under the Affordable Care Act.

Strategies to Reduce Capital Gains Tax

  • Tax-loss harvesting: Sell losing investments to offset gains
  • Hold assets longer than 1 year for the preferential rate
  • Qualified Opportunity Zone investments: Defer and potentially reduce gains
  • Donate appreciated assets to charity — no capital gains, full deduction

Source: IRS Topic No. 409; IRS Rev. Proc. 2024-40

title: Roth IRA vs Traditional IRA: Which Is Right for Your Retirement?
excerpt: Both IRAs offer powerful tax advantages — but at different times. Whether you pay taxes now or later makes a significant difference over decades of compounding.
content:
Both the Roth IRA and Traditional IRA allow your investments to grow tax-advantaged, but they differ fundamentally on when you get the tax break.

Traditional IRA

  • Contributions may be tax-deductible (depending on income and workplace plan)
  • Growth is tax-deferred — no taxes while money grows
  • Withdrawals in retirement are taxed as ordinary income
  • Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs) begin at age 73

Roth IRA

  • Contributions are made with after-tax dollars — no deduction
  • Growth is tax-free
  • Qualified withdrawals in retirement are completely tax-free
  • No RMDs during the owner's lifetime

2024 Contribution Limits (Both)

$7,000 per year ($8,000 if age 50 or older). You can contribute to both if combined total does not exceed the limit.

Roth IRA Income Limits for 2024

  • Single: Phase-out begins at $146,000, ineligible above $161,000
  • MFJ: Phase-out begins at $230,000, ineligible above $240,000

Which Should You Choose?

If you expect to be in a higher tax bracket in retirement, Roth wins. If you expect a lower bracket, Traditional wins. Young earners generally benefit more from Roth; higher earners often prefer Traditional for the immediate deduction.

Source: IRS Publication 590-A; IRS Publication 590-B

title: 401(k) Contribution Limits 2025: How Much Can You Save Tax-Free?
excerpt: The IRS raised 401(k) limits again for 2025. If you have not updated your contribution rate, you may be leaving significant tax savings on the table.
content:
The IRS announced updated retirement plan limits for 2025 in IRS Notice 2024-80 (IR-2024-285). These changes took effect January 1, 2025.

2025 401(k) Limits

  • Employee contribution limit: $23,500 (up from $23,000 in 2024)
  • Catch-up contribution (age 50–59, 64+): Additional $7,500 = total $31,000
  • Super catch-up (ages 60–63): Additional $11,250 = total $34,750 (NEW for 2025 under SECURE 2.0)
  • Total limit including employer contributions: $70,000

IRA Limits (Unchanged for 2025)

  • $7,000 per year ($8,000 if age 50+)

Why This Matters

Every dollar contributed to a traditional 401(k) reduces your taxable income today. At a 22% tax bracket, contributing the full $23,500 saves you $5,170 in federal taxes this year alone — not counting state taxes or the long-term investment growth.

Action Step

Log into your employer's 401(k) portal and update your contribution percentage. Many employers allow changes at any time during the year.

Source: IRS Notice 2024-80; IR-2024-285

title: Rental Property Tax Deductions: What Every Landlord Needs to Know
excerpt: Owning rental property comes with valuable tax deductions that can significantly reduce — or even eliminate — the taxable income from your rental. Here is what qualifies.
content:
Rental income is taxable, but the IRS allows landlords to deduct a wide range of expenses. These deductions are reported on Schedule E of your Form 1040.

Deductible Rental Expenses

  • Mortgage interest: Fully deductible for rental properties
  • Property taxes: Deductible (no $10,000 SALT cap for rental properties)
  • Depreciation: You can depreciate the building (not land) over 27.5 years — one of the most valuable deductions
  • Repairs and maintenance: Deductible in the year incurred (improvements must be capitalized)
  • Insurance premiums: Fully deductible
  • Property management fees: Fully deductible
  • Advertising: Listing fees, photography, signage
  • Professional fees: Accountant and attorney fees related to the rental
  • Travel: Miles driven to manage, maintain, or collect rent
  • Utilities you pay: Fully deductible

Passive Activity Loss Rules

Rental losses are generally passive. You can deduct up to $25,000 in rental losses against ordinary income if your AGI is $100,000 or less. This phases out above $100,000 and disappears at $150,000 AGI.

Repairs vs Improvements

Fixing a broken window is a repair (deduct now). Replacing all windows is an improvement (capitalize and depreciate). The distinction matters for your tax return.

Source: IRS Publication 527; Schedule E Instructions

title: LLC Taxes Explained: How Your Business Entity Affects What You Owe
excerpt: An LLC is a legal structure, not a tax status. The IRS taxes your LLC based on how many members it has and any elections you make. Here is every option explained.
content:
A Limited Liability Company (LLC) protects your personal assets, but the IRS does not have a special tax category for LLCs. Instead, the IRS taxes your LLC based on its default classification or an election you make.

Single-Member LLC (Default)

Treated as a disregarded entity — the IRS ignores the LLC and taxes you directly. You report income and expenses on Schedule C and pay self-employment tax (15.3%) on net profit.

Multi-Member LLC (Default)

Treated as a partnership. The LLC files Form 1065, and each member receives a Schedule K-1 reporting their share of income. Each member pays self-employment tax on their distributive share.

S-Corporation Election

Any LLC can elect S-corp status by filing Form 2553. This allows owners to pay themselves a reasonable salary (subject to payroll taxes) and take additional profits as distributions (not subject to SE tax). This can save thousands for profitable businesses.

C-Corporation Election

LLCs can also elect C-corp status (Form 8832), subjecting profits to the 21% corporate tax rate. Generally only beneficial for businesses retaining significant profits.

Which Is Best?

For most small business owners with net profit above $40,000–$50,000, the S-corp election often provides the greatest tax savings. Consult an Enrolled Agent or CPA to model the numbers for your situation.

Source: IRS Publication 3402; IRS Topic No. 429; Form 2553 Instructions

title: Medical Expense Deduction: What Qualifies and the 7.5% Rule
excerpt: You can deduct medical expenses that exceed 7.5% of your adjusted gross income — but only if you itemize. Knowing what qualifies can mean a significant deduction.
content:
The IRS allows you to deduct qualified medical expenses that exceed 7.5% of your adjusted gross income (AGI), but only if you itemize deductions on Schedule A.

What Qualifies as a Medical Expense?

  • Health insurance premiums (not employer-paid)
  • Doctor, dentist, and hospital visits
  • Prescription medications
  • Vision care (glasses, contacts, LASIK)
  • Mental health services and therapy
  • Medically necessary home improvements (e.g., ramps, lifts)
  • Long-term care insurance premiums (limits apply by age)
  • Mileage to medical appointments (21 cents/mile in 2024)

What Does NOT Qualify?

  • Over-the-counter medications (unless prescribed)
  • Cosmetic surgery not medically necessary
  • Health club dues
  • Vitamins and supplements (unless prescribed)

The 7.5% Threshold Example

If your AGI is $60,000, your threshold is $4,500 (7.5% × $60,000). If you had $8,000 in qualifying medical expenses, you can deduct $3,500 ($8,000 – $4,500).

HSA Strategy

If you have a Health Savings Account (HSA), contributions are pre-tax, withdrawals for medical expenses are tax-free, and the funds roll over indefinitely — making it one of the most tax-efficient ways to pay medical costs.

Source: IRS Publication 502; Schedule A Instructions

title: Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC): Do You Qualify for This Valuable Credit?
excerpt: The EITC is one of the largest refundable credits available to working Americans. Millions of eligible taxpayers miss it every year. Find out if you qualify.
content:
The Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) is a refundable federal tax credit for working individuals with low to moderate income. It can reduce your tax bill to zero and result in a refund even if you owe no tax.

2024 Maximum EITC Amounts

  • No qualifying children: $632
  • 1 qualifying child: $4,213
  • 2 qualifying children: $6,960
  • 3 or more qualifying children: $7,830

2024 Income Limits (Single / Head of Household)

  • No children: $18,591
  • 1 child: $49,084
  • 2 children: $55,768
  • 3+ children: $59,899

Basic Eligibility Rules

  • Must have earned income (wages, self-employment, or farming)
  • Investment income must be $11,600 or less
  • Must have a valid Social Security number
  • Cannot file Married Filing Separately
  • Must be a US citizen or resident alien all year

Common Mistake: Forgetting to Claim It

The IRS estimates that 1 in 5 eligible taxpayers does not claim the EITC. If you think you may qualify, use the EITC Assistant at IRS.gov to check eligibility in minutes.

Source: IRS Publication 596; IRS EITC Central at irs.gov/eitc

title: Gift Tax Rules 2025: How Much Can You Give Tax-Free?
excerpt: Most people who give gifts never owe gift tax — but they may still need to file a return. Understanding the annual exclusion and lifetime exemption prevents costly surprises.
content:
The IRS gift tax applies to transfers of money or property from one person to another without receiving full market value in return. However, most Americans never actually pay gift tax due to the annual exclusion and large lifetime exemption.

Annual Gift Tax Exclusion

  • 2024: $18,000 per recipient
  • 2025: $19,000 per recipient

You can give up to this amount to any number of people each year with no gift tax and no filing requirement. Married couples can combine exclusions to give $38,000 per recipient in 2025.

Lifetime Gift and Estate Tax Exemption

  • 2024: $13,610,000 per person
  • 2025: $13,990,000 per person

Gifts exceeding the annual exclusion reduce your lifetime exemption. Most people will never use up this exemption.

When Do You Need to File Form 709?

File IRS Form 709 (United States Gift and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return) any year you give a gift exceeding the annual exclusion to any one person. Filing the form uses some of your lifetime exemption — it does not necessarily mean you owe tax.

What Is Never Taxable as a Gift?

  • Tuition paid directly to an educational institution
  • Medical expenses paid directly to a healthcare provider
  • Gifts to a spouse (if US citizen) — unlimited
  • Gifts to political organizations

Source: IRS Publication 559; IRS Rev. Proc. 2024-40; Form 709 Instructions

title: How to File a Tax Extension in 2025: Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: Filing a tax extension gives you six more months to file your return — but not six more months to pay. Here is exactly how to request an extension and avoid penalties.
content:
A tax extension gives you until October 15 to file your federal return instead of the standard April 15 deadline. Extensions are automatically granted — you do not need to explain why you need more time.

Critical: Extension to File, Not to Pay

The most important thing to understand: an extension only extends your filing deadline, not your payment deadline. You must still pay any taxes owed by April 15 to avoid the failure-to-pay penalty (0.5% per month) and interest.

How to File Form 4868

  1. Estimate your tax liability for the year
  2. Calculate any amount owed (total tax minus withholding/payments)
  3. Submit Form 4868 by April 15 via:
    • IRS Direct Pay (irs.gov/payments) — mark it as extension payment
    • IRS Free File — submit Form 4868 electronically at no cost
    • Tax software — most major software handles this automatically
    • Mail — send to your regional IRS center (postmarked by April 15)

State Extensions

A federal extension does not automatically extend your state return. Check your state's rules — many states require a separate extension request.

Who Should File an Extension?

Anyone who is missing documents (K-1 from partnerships, foreign tax information, etc.), dealing with a complex tax situation, or simply needs more time to file accurately. There is no penalty for filing an extension.

Source: IRS Form 4868 Instructions; IRS.gov/extensions

title: How to File an Amended Tax Return (Form 1040-X)
excerpt: Made a mistake on your tax return? The IRS allows you to correct it with Form 1040-X. Here is when to file, what to include, and how long it takes.
content:
If you discovered an error on a previously filed tax return — a missed deduction, wrong filing status, unreported income, or overlooked credit — you can correct it by filing Form 1040-X, Amended U.S. Individual Income Tax Return.

When to File an Amended Return

  • You reported income incorrectly
  • You missed a deduction or credit you were entitled to
  • You used the wrong filing status
  • You received a corrected W-2 or 1099 after filing
  • You need to add or remove a dependent

When NOT to File 1040-X

Do not file an amended return to correct math errors — the IRS fixes those automatically. Also, if the IRS sent you a notice correcting an issue, you usually do not need to amend.

Deadline to File

You must file Form 1040-X within 3 years of the original return's due date (or within 2 years of paying the tax, whichever is later). After that, you cannot claim a refund.

How to File

As of 2023, most 1040-X forms can be e-filed through tax software. Otherwise, mail the form to the address listed in the instructions based on your state.

Processing Time

Amended returns take up to 20 weeks to process. Track the status at IRS.gov using the Where's My Amended Return? tool.

Source: IRS Form 1040-X Instructions; IRS.gov/amended-returns

title: US Taxes for Expats: What Americans Living Abroad Must Know
excerpt: The US taxes its citizens on worldwide income regardless of where they live. Expats face unique filing requirements — but also powerful exclusions that can eliminate most of their US tax bill.
content:
The United States is one of only two countries in the world (along with Eritrea) that taxes its citizens on worldwide income, regardless of where they live or where the income is earned.

Who Must File

All US citizens and permanent residents (Green Card holders) living abroad must file a US tax return if their income exceeds the filing threshold — even if they pay taxes in their country of residence.

Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE)

The most powerful tool for expats. For 2024, you can exclude up to $126,500 of foreign earned income (wages, self-employment) from US taxation, provided you meet the Physical Presence Test (330 days outside the US in a 12-month period) or the Bona Fide Residence Test. Claim on Form 2555.

Foreign Tax Credit

If you pay taxes to a foreign government, you can claim a dollar-for-dollar credit on your US return using Form 1116. This prevents double taxation on income not covered by the FEIE.

FBAR and Form 8938

  • FBAR (FinCEN 114): Required if foreign financial accounts exceed $10,000 at any point during the year. Penalties for non-filing: up to $10,000 per violation.
  • Form 8938 (FATCA): Required for foreign assets above $200,000 (single abroad) or $400,000 (MFJ abroad).

Filing Deadline for Expats

Expats get an automatic 2-month extension to June 15, with an additional extension to October 15 available on request.

Source: IRS Publication 54; Form 2555 Instructions; FinCEN 114; Form 8938

title: Back Taxes: What to Do When You Owe the IRS
excerpt: Owing back taxes is stressful — but ignoring the IRS makes it far worse. There are multiple resolution options available, and acting quickly limits penalties and interest.
content:
If you owe back taxes, the worst thing you can do is ignore the IRS. Penalties and interest accumulate daily, and the IRS has significant collection powers — including wage garnishment, bank levies, and liens on property. But there are real solutions available.

File All Unfiled Returns First

Before discussing payment, file every missing return. The failure-to-file penalty is 5% per month on unpaid tax (max 25%) — much steeper than the failure-to-pay penalty of 0.5% per month. Filing stops the larger penalty clock.

Resolution Options

1. Installment Agreement (Payment Plan)

Available for most balances under $50,000. Apply online at IRS.gov. Interest and penalties continue but at reduced rates while in an active agreement.

2. Offer in Compromise (OIC)

Allows you to settle your tax debt for less than the full amount owed — if you can demonstrate that you cannot pay the full liability or that it would cause economic hardship. The IRS accepts roughly 40% of OIC applications. Use the IRS Pre-Qualifier tool at IRS.gov/OIC before applying.

3. Currently Not Collectible (CNC) Status

If you have no ability to pay, the IRS can temporarily suspend collection activity. Interest and penalties continue to accrue, but no collection action is taken.

4. Penalty Abatement

First-time penalty abatement is available to taxpayers with a clean compliance history. Call the IRS or submit Form 843 to request it after paying the tax owed.

The 10-Year Statute of Limitations

The IRS generally has 10 years from the date of assessment to collect a tax debt. After that, the debt expires — though certain actions (like filing for bankruptcy or signing certain agreements) can extend this period.

Source: IRS Collection Procedures; IRS.gov/payments; Form 9465 (Installment Agreement Request); Form 656 (OIC)
